utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to pick up where we left off yesterday, there are available for the Chamber a copy or copies of binders of the type we discussed yesterday. Because the binders were prepared to reflect the indictments, either a binder dealing with deportations or binders dealing with what are described as killing sites individually - and the sample I have before me and which is available to the Chamber relates to the killing site of Bela Crkva - the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's down there, coming up. There are two copies coming up, Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you can introduce this document now, but we don't want to waste too much time. We'll need to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I think it's pretty nearly self-explanatory. It comes, in this particular site, in two volumes. There's an index at the beginning of the first volume. And the only way in which this differs from the binders served on the accused and the amici is that this does not contain the statements it was proposed to tender under 92 bis, whereas their binders did. You'll find within it, as I explained yesterday, a passage from the indictment, an investigator's summary statement, various photographs, maps, and so on, the report of the forensic exhumation team, and associated photographs that connect to that. So that's probably as much as I need say by way of introduction, and if I can invite the Chamber to look at them in due course and return to them when it's convenient. And here's a third copy so that the Chamber can have one each. The second thing, if that's convenient to move on, the second issue that I touched on yesterday and said I'd like leave to return to today relates to the possible amendment of the order in relation to the service of lists of exhibits and witnesses and a pre-trial brief in the Croatia/Bosnia part of the indictment of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Just one moment. It may save some time if we confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can have until the 31st or, rather, the 30th of April, if need be, but no further extensions after that. The Rule will be applied in the usual way, which is that all the material which the Rule requires will have to be provided then. If there are applications to provide further material, of course we would consider them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the Chamber for that, and of course, this is one of those cases where a little more time will enable us to reduce this list, we hope substantially, by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the third point that is outstanding, if I may, because I think it may ultimately save time and be useful, just take a moment or so with it, is the documents that I am proposing to prepare in any event but that I think may be susceptible to a measure of joint preparation or cooperation. There's already before you -- it can be called various things. It can be called a tracking document or a fill-box document, but nevertheless its composition is pretty obvious. This is the fatter document, and it's entirely empty at the moment, but you'll see what it is. It simply takes the indictment and breaks it down, at the moment literally word-for-word. In the vernacular of computer workings, it's cut and paste so that the left-hand column simply takes a part of the indictment, breaks it down, puts it in a box, and then the remaining columns to the right of that allow for the possibility of witness testimony in summary form with transcript page references to fill those boxes. And it becomes particularly important, once we move beyond the introductory paragraphs to the particular identified counts. I'm afraid the pages haven't been page numbered, but that's because the document is at the moment too large to be a single document, but if you go to the third section of the stapled sections, you'll find something that's headed "Forcible Transfer." And so here's the allegations under count 2: Forces of the FRY and Serbia in a deliberate and systematic way did this and that. Witnesses can then be identified in summary form, along with exhibits, and slowly the document will fill up. Now, can I then take you, please, to the sample document that's been very helpfully provided by Mr. Higgins for me, a sample document said to be for display only, which gives an example of how this document may ultimately be valuable to the Trial Chamber. This picks up from paragraph 63(A) of the indictment, Orahovac/Rahovec, sets out on the left-hand side the allegation. On the document, it seems that two witnesses, John and Jane Doe, have given evidence. The summary of their evidence is set out there, the exhibit that they will have produced, and then at the moment in the Comments column it says simply, "No comment." Now, this document, if we prepare it and if it's, for example, subject to corrections by the amici and were the Chamber in a position, through its officers, to suggest any other corrections, could become a document that could be common to all parties as the trial developments. And at the end, that column on the right-hand side, Comments, could of course, become two or three columns and at the closing brief stage, all parties could make their comments and so that the Chamber could see in a snapshot what each party was saying about any particular allegation. This document is, of course, particularly valuable at the end of the Prosecution's case, because at that stage any box that has no entry in it is a box for which there is no evidence and one can then simply immediately concede that that count has not been established. The same material that can be contained on this sort of tracking document, if we look at, say, the witness John Doe, if you now turn to the single sheet, can be set out on another document which simply deals with the same material - that is, a summary of the witness's evidence - at this time witness by witness rather than allegation by allegation. So on the sample page you now have, you see the date is set out. That is the date when the witness gave evidence. The witness's name is set out and the importance of having it in that format is that computer technology would always enable these documents to be resorted so that the witnesses are either dealt with alphabetically or chronologically according to when they were called. There's then the summary of the witness's evidence, matching of course, what would appear on the other document, and then there are various boxes for comments. It's not suggested that these comments should be filled in as the trial is going on. They could, of course, be kept blank until the end of the case. But in the same way as the first document will be susceptible to comments from all relevant parties, providing the Chamber with a snapshot view of the competing arguments about events, you could be provided by this document with a snapshot view of arguments about particular witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what exactly is the purpose of this document? Is it to assist the parties or is it ultimately to be of assistance to the Chamber in its work?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's both. Its principal focus is to assist the Chamber in its work, because my experience is that these documents are -- or something similar are necessary for the parties to prepare in order to make their arguments and likely to be helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the Prosecution comments would be prepared by the Prosecution, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the Defence comments by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the comments by the amici by the amici, and this would reflect their assessment of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, quite frankly, I would not find it appropriate, speaking for myself, because I believe that ultimately it is for the Chamber to assess the evidence, and the Chamber should not be assisted in this way, in my view, by -- by counsel. We will have, at the end of the case, addresses by counsel, and in those addresses, we will their assessment of the evidence. But I personally would find this a little intrusive on my work as a Judge in the Chamber. I prefer to have my own assessment of the evidence. For example, even the summary, who would prepare the summary of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, can I deal with those comments in reverse order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm surprised Your Honour would find it unhelpful to have comments by the parties on the witnesses because, of course, typically at the end of any trial, the parties do provide those comments. One of the problems with cases of this scale is that closing arguments simply cannot deal with every witness and it's never been the case that counsel have been in a position to attempt to do so. In the last case that I appeared in before Your Honour, in a three-hour closing -- a four-hour closing which was permitted to the Prosecution, it was obviously not gong to be possible to provide comments on witnesses one by one. That would have been wholly unrealistic and, indeed, in a 100-page closing brief, it would have been a waste of resources, a waste of available pages to attempt to deal with witnesses individually; and indeed in that case, as the Chamber I think will recall, one of the documents we did provide was a document that provided the sort of comments on witnesses that we hoped would be valuable if the Chamber decided it needed to consider the credibility or so on of any particular witness, typically Defence witnesses in that case. So I'm afraid I stand entirely by the potential utility of this document. It is essential that parties to a criminal trial are in a position to make their submissions about witnesses or about evidence available to the Chamber, but in trials of this scale, it is necessary to take imaginative steps to enable that to happen without seeking wholly excessive periods of time in oral argument to present the material. Further, there can be no unfairness -- Your Honour asked me was this to help the Chamber or to help the parties. There can be no unfairness because one of the particular purposes of this document is to enable the accused, who is unrepresented, to have a way of marshalling his comments, if he wishes so to do, and present them to the Chamber in a way that could be readily accessible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me give you an example of what I mean. John Doe, 2nd of May. There is a summary. The summary is presumably prepared by -- by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was coming to that. That would be prepared by us, but as I've already said, it could be the subject of discussion with the amici, it could be the subject, if the Chamber so decided, with those who prepare such documents for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I really believe that would be highly questionable. I mean, as a document for the parties themselves, yes, but, for example, Prosecution comments on John Doe, "Doe was a credible witness." That's what I would expect the Prosecution to say. It is still a matter for the Chamber ultimately to decide on the credibility of the witness. So that wouldn't take us very far. The Chamber would still have to read that witness's evidence and assess the credibility of the witness. So I don't see how a statement from the Prosecution that Doe was a credible witness who could provide first-hand testimony would be very helpful because that is a matter which the Chamber itself would have to determine after reading the evidence in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, and the particular comments here may not be typical of the comments you would receive. The comments you might receive, for example, following Mr. Ryneveld's careful examination of the witness yesterday might include such things as: Witness omitted passages X, Y and Z, drawn to the Chamber's attention. Notwithstanding that, Chamber invited to approach witness on this basis. Precisely the comments that, in this type of trial, are made by counsel to the Judge, or to a jury, to the Judge at the end of the process. This is designed to be helpful. It's designed to enable, in a manageable way, the duties of counsel, prosecuting and appearing for the amici, to be performed in a setting where the accused will not be disadvantaged by his being unrepresented. Now, as to the summary, of course the summary, which will attempt to be neutral and fair, will come from one of the parties. Somebody's got to take the initiative. And I'm quite content to stop at any negotiations, as it were, with the amici themselves and to present the document in that form. What I am concerned about, and let me be quite blunt about this, what I am concerned about is that in a case -- in cases of this sort, it may inevitably be that a Chamber will proceed in due course in part on summaries. It is infinitely preferable, in our respectful submission, that wherever possible, the summary or a summary upon which the Chamber may proceed can be a transparent document, looked at and considered by all parties, and in particular by the Defence. So that our proposal remains, if I may say so, one that we invite you to consider helpful, constructive, and positive, a proposal that we should prepare a document in broadly these forms or this form --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the comment you just made goes to the very heart of the matter, which is that the -- in your view, in your respectful submission, the Chamber should, wherever possible, proceed on a summary which is a transparent document. The Chamber proceeds on the basis of the evidence given in court. That is what the Chamber proceeds on, not on the basis of any summary. And if the Chamber has a summary, it must be the Chamber's own summary. It can't be a summary which -- in which the parties have participated in the preparation of, in my view. And we'll hear your submissions, but ultimately, it is for the Chamber, on an assessment of the evidence, to determine the credibility of the witness, the trustworthiness of each witness. I'm not inflexible on this, and we'll take the document and we'll consider it, but those are the views I have at this moment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think we've heard -- we have your points. This is essentially a closing brief for the Prosecution. Now, it may well be extremely useful as a document to put before us if there's a submission at half-time. It may be extremely useful as a document instead of a closing brief or attached to a closing brief in which you set out your summary, your list of evidence on a particular point, your comments about the witnesses. All that we accept. But I think we are agreed that, as a working document, it is not going to be of assistance to us. In fact, the Chamber must do its own work and its own assessment, as it will. It will be assisted by the Chamber -- by the parties where necessary. In particular, it's not an appropriate course, it seems to me, in a case in which the accused is in person. It would be different, perhaps, if he was represented, but there again, that's open to argument. But since he's in person, it isn't. If the amicus, on reflection, wish to add something to the schedule and are prepared to do that, then of course, that might be helpful, but it would be a matter for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm grateful for the expression of views and I take no more time than, if I may, just two points. One, of course, in answer to His Honour Judge Robinson's point, I wasn't saying that it was inevitable and desirable that you would proceed on a summary. Obviously, and we know this from the judgements that we receive, the Chamber must go back to the transcript but it gets to the transcript via a document and this may be a document that would be helpful. So that's the first point. And the second point is that this is not in answer to His Honour Judge May's characterisation. Although this would become part of the Prosecution brief, as it has done in other cases, its purpose and the reason I raise it now includes that it can help the accused, who has chosen to be unrepresented, to present his comments in an orderly way that might assist you, because otherwise, you may not have his comments available in that form. What I'll do is I'll carry on preparing this document, I'll negotiate with the amici and see if they wish to receive it from time to time. If they do, then the document will have that perhaps additional value at the time we come to present it, as we will, as part of our closing. Thank you for the time in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Hence we will return the documents, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That leaves 92 bis and the scope of cross-examination I think now for next week. Ms. Romano will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There may be some matters the amicus wants to raise and also the accused who was told he would have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, very briefly, I must admit that I did not quite understand the idea that was presented by Mr. Geoffrey Nice, because I think that evidence has to be produced here before you. It has to be fully presented here. And then while it is presented, objections may be raised. And I certainly cannot understand that Mr. Nice speaks of imagination when evidence is concerned. That is my main objection. And I think that when evidence is produced, we are going to react to evidence that is on the table right then, and that is the only way I think we can proceed in this case. In view of your ruling that has to do with us, the amici curiae, that you addressed to us on the 11th of January, 2002, where you said quite clearly that we should assist the Trial Chamber in every possible way that we deem appropriate at that moment. Yesterday I discussed this only very briefly with Mr. Kay during the proceedings. You have heard Slobodan Milosevic already twice here before you and once on that day when the hearing was held before the Appeals Chamber. He asked for his own release but not release for the sake of freedom as such but primarily freedom that would make it possible for him to be on a footing of equality with the opposing party. You are fully aware of the fact that this is the first case in which a person is defending himself on his own completely. The Court is indeed in a delicate situation. You know that Rule 45 envisages the possibility that Milosevic opted for, but at this moment, I would like to focus the attention of the Trial Chamber on the Statute, the Statute of the Tribunal that says that every accused must be provided a minimum guarantee of having adequate time and resources to prepare his defence. This is the Serbian version, and I don't think the translation is proper. I'm going to read from the French version now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, would you just pause a minute. If you're going to make an application for provisional release, as you seem to be, I'm not sure that this is the right time to be doing it. It may be appropriate -- when we have got witnesses waiting. It may be appropriate later. But let me consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very brief, Judge May, very brief. That is not my point right now, although we have to think about that as well, and perhaps the Trial Chamber should give due consideration to this as well at some point. What I wish to say now is that we have to find the ways and means of enabling Slobodan Milosevic to be prepared for every day in court when evidence is being produced. I don't know what kind of proposal I should submit to you at this point in time. I don't know whether these should be counsellors that he would select, that he would be in a position to contact every day and whether these consultations can take place at the detention unit. However, the point of this is that what Slobodan Milosevic said yesterday, that he does not even have access to the telephone and that he needs to deal with what has been dealt with in Court. So I'm not insisting on provisional release right now and the equality of arms, so to speak, but the Trial Chamber should simply find ways and means of enabling Slobodan Milosevic, since he is unrepresented anyway, to prepare properly for every day in court. That is the point I wish to make now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you have a concrete proposal, we'll hear it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something straightaway? In January, you allowed free discussions between Slobodan Milosevic and counsellors he did not accept. However, if he has advisors that he does accept, then he should simply be in a position to talk to them, to discuss things with them, and to see how he is going to act in certain situations since he is defending himself anyway. We do not have any contact with Slobodan Milosevic. You know that we are not avoiding this contact and we can have this contact on the basis of your ruling, but we deem that this would be necessary one way or the other, and that is the point I wish to make to you right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, in the light of what you just said, are you saying that there is anything now that stands in the way of Mr. Milosevic having contact with his associates and other people to provide him assistance? If that is so, I would consider that a very serious matter which would require very urgent attention by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Robinson, first and foremost, that is a problem that he indicated to you yesterday, that he does not even have telephone links to anyone any longer. But I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not so. He does have telephone links.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. However, telephone is insufficient for this kind of thing. I think that a solution can be found. The Trial Chamber can certainly find a solution for this. If Slobodan Milosevic wishes to say free contacts, unhindered contacts with his advisors, there should be no problem in this regard. He should be put in this position, to have this minimum guarantee for preparing properly for the proceedings here. I don't think that there should be a problem in this regard within the boundaries and the limits in the prison, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... it will certainly have my full support, because as you say, that's a right which he has not only under the Statute, but under customary international law to have adequate facilities for the preparation of his defence. But let us know concretely what it is that you have in mind. The telephone matter, as far as I am aware, as far as the Chamber is aware, has been addressed. If there is still a problem with the telephone, then let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to keep you any longer. I shall try, together with my colleagues, to perhaps write some submissions to this effect, but this seems to be a problem to me -- a problem that, to my mind, requires a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You were told you would have an opportunity to raise any matters. You can do so now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would -- I would like to continue along identical lines, perhaps not altogether identical, regarding this subject that has been raised by one of the amici curiae. You know full well that the fundamental right that is guaranteed by the international covenant on international political and civil rights, and there is a European, an African, an American declaration to this effect, a basic right is the right to defence. I have fully been denied this right through this isolation, and it is quite clear that no mention can be made of a fair trial here or equality of arms. I have no conditions whatsoever for defending myself here. On the other hand, all of you know full well that I am not going to run away from this place of force and injustice, where my people and where my country are being defended, because these are the gravest possible accusations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are not impressed by your political points. You have made them a great many times. They do not improve with repetition. Now, if you have a serious application to make to this Trial Chamber, will you make it? Tell us what it is you're asking for, and we will consider it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very seriously, there is not a more serious question that I am raising, more serious than that one, and that is for you to release me, and you know full well that I'm not going to escape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will consider that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do. Furthermore, I wish to make a comment. I assume that you have given me that right as well. I would like to comment on these proposals that we've heard from the Prosecution, and also I would like to make a comment on the comment made by one of the amici. I think that I quite understand what the other side wants, the one that submitted this false indictment. That side wants to organise the work of both sides, both parties. They even want to organise the work of the Trial Chamber with this idea of some kind of a document that is supposed to serve the interests of all three sides and that one side will hold and manage and in this way it is already in a position to hold an entire machinery in their own hands as opposed to the other side what has been denied its right to defend itself. So they even want to improve upon their already advantageous position. We have heard yesterday, from the explanations provided by the Prosecutor, that I practically bother them here by everything I've been doing and saying here. Now I see that they're bothered by the existence of the Trial Chamber as well, because they want to give instructions to the Trial Chamber as to how they are going to judge the authenticity of what they have been presenting. In this way, they wish to compensate for the fact that their evidence is totally amiss. These are false witnesses. Even Judge Robinson, as far as I have understood things, made a comment to the effect that the Prosecutor went too far by making such a submission. I should say that this is putting it very mildly when commenting upon what the Prosecutor has done. It is quite clear that, with this idea, the Prosecutor wants the Prosecution to take over for both parties; that is to say, to take over my function as well, and perhaps even yours, that of the Trial Chamber. Perhaps the best thing would be is if all would refrain from their activities whatsoever and that the Prosecution pronounce their ruling, their decision on the basis of all these verbal resources that are being used to deny material facts. In order to make a comparison to what they have been doing, Osama bin Laden could bring you as many witnesses, also from Kosovo and Metohija, who could swear that they saw with their own eyes, George Bush throwing grenades and bombs on the Pentagon and the White House. Verbal resources cannot be used to altogether annul something that has been seen by the entire world. This cannot annul the activities of the KLA or the NATO aggression, especially not in this way in which the Prosecutor has been working with his ambition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm -- Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to stop you now. You've made your point. In fact, we had already ruled that we are not going to look at that document. What we've said is this: The Prosecution can produce the document at the end of the proceedings when it will be part of their submissions to the Trial Chamber. That is all it will be. And the fears you've expressed, you need have no trouble about. The Trial Chamber are not going to look at it. Thank you very much. Let's hear the witnesses now. Sorry, there is one matter Judge Robinson wants to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you remember yesterday I commended Mr. Tapuskovic for the role that he played in cross-examining a witness on the witness statement. I commended him because he was endeavouring to pinpoint in the witness statement information or evidence which tended to contradict what the witness said in court. Now, he did that because you have taken the position not to read the witness statement, and that is -- that's your right. But I want to suggest to you that your interests would be better served by reading the witness statements which are, in fact, not very long, for this reason: The witness statements will quite often contain information and evidence which might contradict what is said in court, and you would be in a better position to make better use of that contradiction than the amicus curiae, for the very simple reason that you have more information about the matters than the amicus. So I want to leave it to you for your consideration that in the interests of your defence, you would be well advised to read the witness statements in putting forward your case before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Besnik Sokoli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, would you please state your full name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: My name is Besnik Sokoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Sir, you were born on the 2nd of September, 1977, in Peja; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What's your current profession?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I'm a professional translator.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where do you work?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm working for the UNMIK police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where did you work before?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: During 1998, I worked for the US KDOM observer, then for the OSCE, and after the war, I worked for the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What was your work for the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I worked as a field interpreter for the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, can you briefly describe to the Court where Peja is located.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Peja is in the west of Kosova and borders on Montenegro. The nearest villages are Raushiq and Vitromirica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of Peja before March 1999?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I believe that about 90 per cent were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, how would you describe the situation in Peja or near Peja during the summer 1998 and to March 1999?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: It was very tense, especially after certain incidents that happened. And as a staff member for the OSCE, I suffered some mistreatment, and the Serbs who lived in Peja attacked OSCE cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will stop you for a minute, Mr. Sokoli. Let's go back to when you started saying that it was tense because certain incidents. Can you describe what kind of incidents?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact dates, but I think it was December, and there was an incident when six Serbs were killed in a cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you know who killed the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know. But according to rumours that I've heard, there was a certain -- there was a certain argument among the Serbs themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what was the argument?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I don't -- I think you didn't understand my question, Mr. Sokoli. Do you know what was the argument that they were exchanging among themselves?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So what happened after this incident?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Until that incident, we went to work more freely - I'm talking of myself - but after this incident, we were the -- the observers had to come and fetch us from our homes, and we were shut up in our homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: At that time, you were working for the KVM mission?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: The OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: At that time, was the Serb army present in Peja, during 1998 and before March 1999?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. There was the police together with the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And were they -- what was the police and army doing together?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I don't know how to reply. They were there, as I said. There was some mistreatment of the Albanian population by Serbian civilians, and there were also excesses in which the police and the army mistreated Albanian citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember or can you tell the Court an example of any mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: For example, the day after the incident I described earlier, in the centre of Peja, a lot of Albanians were beaten by Serbian civilians, and the police were present but didn't intervene in any way at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, were you or any members of your family associated to the KLA at any time?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And was the KLA present in your town?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that the KLA was in the city of Peja, and the only information I have about the KLA I obtained from the media and the television. They were mostly deployed among the hills and the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing them coming to -- to the town? I mean to Peja.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, not before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And after the war?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them -- I saw members of the KLA after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you know about fights between the Serb forces and the KLA between -- during 1998?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Have you witnessed any of these fights?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So how did you become aware of the fights?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Through the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What kind of media?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I think news such as the BBC and EuroNews and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, I will turn right now to the 24 of March, when the NATO bombing started in Kosovo. Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: At this time I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: In Peja?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes, in Peja.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And was Peja hit or bombed that day?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where were you on the next day of NATO bombing, on the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I was still at home on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were you alone at home?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No. I was with my family and also with the Bobi family, my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How many people total in your house?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you leave your house?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I left my home on 28th of March, Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So while you were at your home on the 25th of March, what did you see or hear?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: On the 24th and 25th, it was relatively calm, but on the evening of the 25th and on the 26th and 27th, there was shelling in a neighbourhood near my neighbourhood called Zatra, and I saw several houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You could see this from your house?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you see the shelling?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I saw flames and the glow from the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did at any time you leave, you leave your house?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: On the 27th of March, my father went to the gate of the house and saw the police who were there with an APC, as he told me. And on the next day, in the morning, I, on the 28th, I went to the gate and I didn't see anybody, not even my neighbours, and we decided to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What was the reason why your neighbours went away? What was the situation at that time?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I don't know why they left, but at that time, I was very scared, and I was frightened to remain there with my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So you remained in your house for two days, and you said that on the 28th of March, you left. So can you describe what happened on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, Sunday, we went together, my family and the Bobi family, went to my aunt's house in another part of the city, in a neighbourhood called Gjemajl Kada. We went through the lanes so that the police and army we wouldn't see us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And while you were heading to this place, what did you see or hear?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I noticed a large police presence; burned houses; looted, broken shops; and all their property stolen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, let's go back to what you said about the large police presence. How many policemen did you see at that time?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I can't give a number because they were always moving, but I would say more than 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And how were they dressed? Did they have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. They were in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniform?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: It was a blue camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia or patch?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: On the left arm, they had "Milicija" written.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Could I please have the witness shown Exhibit number 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, I will ask you to look at this series of photos and indicate to the Court if you -- if you find any uniforms similar to the ones you saw that day.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: It was this one, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you describe the weapons?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I again have the witness shown Exhibit 21 this time. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, please, if you can, take a look in this series of photos and indicate if you can identify any of the weapons that you saw them carrying at that time.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Which number is that?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Number 3 is similar to that, but I'm unable to define it more exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Sokoli. So it's number 3 from sheet B?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sokoli, can you describe, what did you see the police doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: It was very difficult, and I was trying not to be seen. They were always in movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you hear shooting or did you see fire?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I saw flames from the houses, and I also heard shots which seemed to me to be further away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You said that your neighbourhood was deserted. Were there people in the streets as well at the same time that you were leaving?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No. Besides the police, I didn't see anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So from your house, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I went to my aunt, as I said, in the Gjemajl Kada neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How far was your aunt's house from your house?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: About 40 minutes on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So during all these 40 minutes was the time when you saw the police moving around?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did you -- did you speak with anybody else while you were in the street; with any other villagers?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, because I didn't see anybody. I was with my family and with the Bobi family.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: After you arrived in your aunt's house, were you able to see what was happening from your aunt's house?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Besides smoke from the houses, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left your aunt's house?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: After an hour, I heard people on foot outside the house, in great panic. I went out and asked what was happening, and they told me that the police and the army were come and were killing and were burning houses, looting and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So that was the reason why you decided to leave again?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes, because it was terrible even to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Then my family and the Bobi family decided to walk to the first town in Montenegro, to Rozaje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So what did you see or hear while you were walking?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Again, I saw a large police presence in several places. They didn't stop me and didn't stop me until the reached the crossroads for the road to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you reach the border to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: The police stopped me at this crossroads. There were five or six of them in the same uniform, and they told me that I couldn't continue on this road.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did they tell you why?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No. They didn't give me a real answer, but I insisted, and I lied to them, saying that their colleagues had told me to go in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what did they do?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: [In English] They were very -- [Interpretation] They were very aggressive and told me that I had to go back to the centre of Peja, where they had organised buses and trucks to leave the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So did you go back to Peja?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. I went back to the centre of Peja.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you walk back to Peja?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I walked for a bit and then a car stopped which took me and my parents, and to the -- even today, I still don't know who this person was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So when you arrived in Peja, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: When we arrived in Peja near the Metohija Hotel, we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: There was a great crowd of Albanian civilians; about 30.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So why were you gathered in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: All the citizenry had been told the same, to gather in the centre where buses and trucks would take them from the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What kind of buses and trucks?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: They were civilian buses and trucks. They belonged to various Albanian private travel agencies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, who told the citizens that the buses and the trucks were coming?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And do you know -- do you know where the buses and the trucks came from, if they belonged to any company?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: The two companies I remember, one was TRY Turs and the other was Flamengo Turs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Who was driving the buses and the trucks?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: The police themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately how many buses and trucks?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I think about eight.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And at that time, were the police present?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. There was a large number of policemen there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: They were there and were directing the people who would go into buses and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were they telling the people where the buses were going to?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I didn't hear this, nor did I hear anything like this, except in one of the trucks, there was a piece of paper marked Rozaje, which is a town in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing any police or military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. There were policemen moving with civilian cars and also with armoured vehicles and police cars. But I also saw two large tanks of the army. I think they were the army's because they were green.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I please have the witness shown Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Sir, can you please examine the -- this series of photos and again indicate if you can identify any of the vehicles that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: The tank was about of this size.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You're showing number 6.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How many tanks did you see?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I saw two arriving at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did you see any military -- any - sorry - police vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. I saw blue armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you see any similar photo in this series of photos that you have before you?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: They were approximately of this kind, but they were blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness indicated number 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recognise any other vehicles that you saw present in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I saw a red Mercedes which was driving by.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, can you describe what the citizens were doing at that time in the town, what was happening? They were going into the buses?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: There was a great panic, fear. My mother was standing close to me. She wanted to protect me from the police staring at me or looking at me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did you see other citizens getting into the buses and being driven away?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And were the buses coming back to get more people?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. About two hours and a half or three hours, the same buses and trucks returned to get other citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What happened to you, Mr. Sokoli, at that time?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: At about 3.00, six policemen came and they took me to a hotel called Metohija then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What happened in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: They maltreated me physically and psychologically.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes, they did beat me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Mostly on the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you know why they were beating you?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were they saying anything to you?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. They were asking me, "Where is KLA?" "Where is NATO now?" And they kept asking me questions like, "If we give you an insignia against NATO, a slogan against NATO, would you dare go in front of the citizens and hold it up in the air?"

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What happened to you next?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: This lasted for about five or six hours. Then the buses and trucks came again and something happened outside, I didn't know what, some panic amongst the people. And the six policemen left the room and left me alone. In a minute or so, another policeman came, and he seized me by the arm and dragged me to the truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you recognise this man?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I saw him in the past, or earlier. He was carrying a bag with the Red Cross sign on it. He was not armed. He impressed me because he spoke with children who were there in the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where did he take you to?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: He took me out of the hotel and asked me to get inside one of the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: At that time, did you know where your family was?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: My family was in the same truck, vehicle with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How many people were in the truck?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: About 60 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I saw a sign put on this truck, "Rozaje," but they took us to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember who was driving the bus?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: At that moment, I didn't see who, but when we arrived in Prizren, I saw that he was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When you arrived in Prizren, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: When we approached the entrance to Prizren and on the way to Albania, I saw a large police presence and civilians, Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, when you say "police," can you identify the uniforms? Can you describe the uniforms, if they were wearing one?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. They were dressed in the same uniform I described earlier, that is, blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: At that moment, some of the citizens began to walk in the direction of Albania. Meanwhile, one of the policemen shouted, telling them to stop. And he told us that some other buses are going to take us closer to the border with Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people were with you in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I'm not sure. About 600 or 700.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did more trucks or buses arrive?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No. Until we were there, no, I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So from Prizren, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: From Prizren, some other buses arrived there, and they took us to a village. I don't remember the name. It was somewhat five kilometres away from Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And were the buses the same or different buses?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: They were other buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did you see who was driving those buses as well?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. They were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And do you remember approximately how many buses?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: About five or six, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did the police who were guiding you to go into the buses, you and the other citizens?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: The police were there, telling us to go into the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So after you got in one of the buses, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: After we got on the bus, we were driven up to the village I said earlier. Then we walked on foot up to the border.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, before crossing the border, did you have to show or did you have to give any of your documents?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. The policemen were there, and they asked the people to give them their IDs and passports they had on them, or any other identification documents they had, and I saw that they pulled off the licence plates from the cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, when you say "policemen," can you again describe their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. The same uniforms; blue camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How many policemen did you see at the border?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: About 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did they tell the people why they have to have hand over their documents?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did they also tell why they were taking out the plates from the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Albania?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I arrived in Albania - in Kukes, to be more precise - on the 29th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When did you return to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I came alone - I don't remember, it was 16th or 17th - to see what was left of our own house or my job -- my property. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And how did you find your house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 16th or 17th of which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How did you find your house?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: The top was burned and everything was looted and raided from my property.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Last question, Mr. Sokoli: Why did you leave Kosovo and went to Albania?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I was obliged to leave Kosova out of fear, because I used to work for the OSCE, and we were the target of the police and military. I was afraid that something bad might happen to my family and to myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You said you worked with the OSCE. What was the role of the OSCE at that time?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: The OSCE played the role of observer to ensure a security, a safe environment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And why do you think you was -- you were a target by working with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Because when I was in the OSCE car, which had orange colour, we often were thrown stones at by Serbian civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, did you leave because of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I did not leave because of NATO bombing, because I didn't have any reason to be afraid of them. My house was not situated close to the police stations or police barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sokoli, we're going to adjourn now for half an hour. Would you be back, please, at 11.30 for further examination. Would you remember in this break and other others there may be in your evidence not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prior to the beginning of your work with the KVM, have you always lived in Pec?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you spent some time in Switzerland and Germany prior to that?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: In Germany, I was in 1992 for a short visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the rest of the time you spent in the country?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From 1992 until 1998, without any interruption, meaning you didn't go abroad, did you?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I haven't been abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that 90 -- the population of Pec was 90 per cent Albanian.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But based on the existing figures, 76 per cent of the population of Pec was Albanian.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I said approximately, but I do not know exactly the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, let us go back to the events that you've described. I will start with the most recent events you described at the end. You described the events from the 24th until the 29th of March, when you crossed into Albania. Was Pec a war zone during those days?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The NATO aggression started on the 24th, and for a number of months prior to that, there were clashes with the KLA formations. During those days, as you were leaving Pec, was Pec already a war zone?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: As I've said earlier, there were no KLA forces in Peja town, but I do not know of any other war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll go back to the KLA forces at a later stage. The entire border zone during those days was a war zone, in fact. You described refugees that were leaving the war zone, therefore, would it be true to conclude that soldiers and policemen helped you and other civilians to leave the war zone?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I don't think so, because -- because I was beaten up and mistreated and so were other citizens. And I did not leave Kosova for any other reason other than being frightened of something happening to me from the Serb police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you only about the facts. They asked you whether you wanted to carry an anti-NATO slogan. That's what you said, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you reply to them?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I answered yes, because if I were to have said no, I couldn't have imagined the consequences, what would have happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you wanted to go from your town towards Rozaje, meaning to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No. I did not want to go anywhere, but the circumstances forced me to take a decision during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you started with your parents in the direction of Rozaje and that at the crossroads you were turned back by the police in order to board the buses rather than walk. That's the explanation you gave us here, therefore, you were walking in the direction of Rozaje.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: We decided to go to Rozaje because it was close by, and we thought it would be safer if we went there and take shelter for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The territory of Montenegro was less bombed than the entire territory of Serbia, and even less than the territory of Kosovo. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I'm thinking about the NATO bombing in Serbia and Montenegro. All of that, I've followed these events through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this fact pertaining to your departure to Rozaje has something to do with the bombing as well, and the question I have for you is as follows: Do you know that on the 25th of March the area of Rozaje was bombed? I have a fact here concerning a young man, a Muslim young man, Senat Dacic, a 16-year-old who was killed, and I also have information about a large number of wounded persons. Therefore, this is why you were turned back from that road that wasn't safe, because on that occasion, cluster bombs were used. Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, on the road that you wanted to use to go from Pec to Rozaje, cluster bombs were used. This is why that road was not considered to be safe for refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, he said he doesn't know about that. Perhaps -- perhaps the witness can help us with this: When the police turned you back, did they say anything about bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They didn't tell us anything of that sort or of bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, do your answers suggest that the authorities did not allow Albanians to go to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I can't talk about their intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that several tens of thousands of refugees from Kosovo and Metohija went to Montenegro, using that very road, but later on, when there were no cluster bombs on that road? Do you know that several tens of thousands of citizens went, using that same road, to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I also don't know when they left Kosova, but I learned through the media that several thousand refugees took shelter in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, because -- since you worked in the Verification Mission, you should know that there are figures of the UNHCR concerning the number of refugees. Are you aware of that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I can't answer yes or no but simply, through the media, I know that there were figures about different numbers of refugees who had taken refuge in different cities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said at the beginning that the tensions in Pec were caused by what you called an incident in the Panda cafe in Pec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he said that. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That incident took place on the 14th of December, 1998. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I said before I remember the month but not the exact day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you remember that it was in December of 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that it was December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you believe that, prior to that, there were no incidents that would lead to increased tension?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I don't know of any in the city of Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a relative thing. Do you know that from May until November of 1998, meaning from May until November of 1998, that the police had clashes with the KLA in a large number of villages around Pec? For example, the village of Lodza is two kilometres from Pec, Lubeniq also two, Rausic five kilometres, Streoc 10 kilometres, Breznik and so on. Six members from MUP were killed. So do you have knowledge of these attacks of the KLA on the police and civilians in general from May until November of 1998? All these events took place in the area of Pec.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: In the connection with the KLA, I said before that they were in the hills and woods or in villages, and I believe that they were opposed by Serbian forces. And all these things that I'm saying now are things that I've heard from the media. They were in the forests, and they were helping the populous who had been expelled from their villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked specifically about incidents in the villages around Pec during which, as I understand it, it's alleged that six members of the MUP were killed. Do you have any knowledge of any such incidents? If you don't, say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know about these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, for example, about an incident in the Karagaq Hotel Park in Pec - this is an area of Pec - when the representatives of the OSCE mission came to verify the rumours as to what was going on in that hotel, and they talked to the deputy commander of the KLA brigade, who happened to be there?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you used to work at the Verification Mission. Therefore, I suppose that you, as an employee of the Verification Mission, had more information available to you than the rest of the population. Did you have any information regarding this or not?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I didn't have information regarding this incident. And as for the Verification Mission in Kosovo, I worked as a supervisor of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were no incidents in Pec. And in order to save the time, I will ask you just about the Albanians. Do you know that on the 26th of May, 1998, in the town itself, in Pec, so on the 26th of May, 1998, Komanica Dela was killed? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 2nd of June, another Albanian was killed in Pec, therefore in the downtown as well, and his name is Thaci Uka?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 3rd of June, another Albanian was killed, Zyber Berisha, near the Pec patriarchy?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 24th of June, Adem Gjuka and Baki Gjuka were killed?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know only about that incident. And do you know about the event that took place on August 1st, when Zenun Gashi was killed?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Veton Kelmendi was killed on the 2nd of January.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Rrustem Sadriu was killed on the 11th of January?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Emin Basha was killed on the 31st of January. Have you heard about this murder?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the 10th of February, Qerim Suka was killed. You haven't heard about that either, have you?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You used to work at the Verification Mission. Do you know that in the Verification Mission's report - this is the OSCE mission - pertaining to the period between 10th and 11th of March, 1999 -- from 9th until 12th of March, 1998, it says that pursuant to the KLA command structure's order, more Albanians who were loyal to Serbia were killed. Do you know about this report and do you know that this is what the report says? This was the report of the Verification Mission where you used to work.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No. I have not seen such reports nor heard anything of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that you were not afraid of the bombing because you didn't live near the barracks or the police station. And do you know that, during the aggression, there were not troops in Pec because they all left towards the area near the water? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, in those days, there were 18 funerals of policemen from Pec who were killed by the KLA? This is something that people usually take note of, the funerals. Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a large number of Albanians and a huge majority of Muslims and Romany remained in Pec during the aggression, as did a large number of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: When I came back after the war and after the entry of the NATO forces in Kosova, I found no Albanians, Romanies, or Muslims in Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, when you came back, Pec was empty. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: Yes. I only met a few soldiers of Italian KFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since, according to you, you were in Pec at that time, did you see that 90 per cent of the Serb houses in Pec were burned down at precisely the time when you came back to Pec?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: When I returned, I only saw my own neighbourhood and several neighbourhoods that I know, and a lot of Albanian houses were burned. I didn't notice anything about Serbian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't know that 90 per cent of the Serb houses in Pec were burned down?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all Serb villages in the Pec environs were burnt down? For example, Crni Vrh, Ljuljosa, Brestovik, Vitanica, and so on? Do you know that all Serb villages in the environs of Pec were burnt down?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: After I returned to Peja, there was -- there was a very small number of Serbian houses that were burned, and as for the vacated and burned villages, I don't know about these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But later, the remaining Serb houses were burned down. I assume that you should know about that. Do you know about that or do you not know about that?

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: No, they weren't burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you started out with the explanation that tensions in Pec were caused by the incident, as you called it, at the Cafe Panda, and that all these events and all these killed people from May until December, because this event occurred on the 14th of December, are something that you are not aware of, and they did not create any tension whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a comment, really, on the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just asking. He started out by the tensions caused by that incident, as he had called it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim, in respect of this truly horrible crime that all of Yugoslavia's aware of, that it was as a result of a quarrel amongst Serbs.

utterances.speaker: BESNIK SOKOLI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your evidence was that, as you understood it, there was a quarrel between Serbs which led to this incident in which six people were killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said were rumours that I heard from citizens in Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
